title: Data, summary statistics and regression
summary: Sampling and presenting data, measures of centre and spread, outliers, and describing bivariate data with Pearson’s and Spearman’s correlation and a regression line.

keyterms.definition: The population is the whole group of interest; a sample is the subset actually studied.
Discrete data take separate countable values; continuous data can take any value in a range.
Every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen.
Sampling at random from each subgroup in proportion to its size.
A systematic tendency of a sampling method or measurement to misrepresent the population.
A value more than 1.5 × IQR below Q1 or above Q3.
A diagram of the five-number summary: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum.
Measures of central tendency: the average, the middle value and the most frequent value.
IQR = Q3 − Q1, the spread of the middle 50% of the data.
σ, a measure of the typical distance of data from the mean (found with a GDC).
r, between −1 and 1, measuring the strength and direction of linear correlation.

keyterms.term: Regression line of y on x
keyterms.definition: The least-squares line y = ax + b used to predict y from x within the data range.
Predicting outside the range of the data; usually unreliable.
rₛ: Pearson’s r applied to the ranks; measures how monotonic a relationship is.

questions.prompt: Which of these is discrete data?
questions.explanation: Counts take separate values; measurements are continuous.

questions.text: In ___ random sampling every member of the population has an equal chance of selection.
questions.explanation: Simple random sampling needs a full list of the population.

questions.statement: Convenience sampling is likely to be biased.
questions.explanation: Choosing whoever is easy to reach rarely represents the whole population.

questions.prompt: A school has 600 students, 240 of them in Grade 11. A stratified sample of 50 is taken. How many Grade 11 students are chosen?
Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 32. Which value is an outlier?
questions.explanation: IQR = 12, so the fences are 20 − 18 = 2 and 32 + 18 = 50. Only 52 lies outside.

questions.statement: The median can be estimated from a cumulative frequency graph by reading across at half the total frequency.
questions.explanation: Reading at n/4 and 3n/4 gives the quartiles.

questions.prompt: Match each sampling method to its description.

pairs.right: every kth item from a list
fixed numbers from groups, chosen non-randomly
random sample from each subgroup in proportion

questions.explanation: Knowing the difference lets you criticise a method’s bias.

questions.prompt: A box and whisker plot displays:
questions.explanation: Minimum, Q1, median, Q3 and maximum (with outliers marked separately).

questions.prompt: Put the five-number summary in order.
questions.explanation: These are the points shown on a box plot.

questions.text: Data that can take any value in a range, such as height, are ___.
questions.explanation: Continuous data come from measuring rather than counting.

questions.prompt: Find the mean of 4, 7, 7, 9, 13.
Find the median of 4, 7, 7, 9, 13.
questions.explanation: The middle (3rd) value of the ordered list is 7.

questions.text: The population standard deviation σ of 4, 7, 7, 9, 13 is about ___.
questions.explanation: σ² = 44/5 = 8.8 and σ = √8.8 ≈ 2.97. 3.32 is the sample value sₙ₋₁.

questions.statement: Adding 5 to every value increases the mean by 5 but leaves the standard deviation unchanged.
questions.explanation: Shifting the data does not change how spread out it is.

questions.prompt: Every value in a data set is doubled. What happens to the standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Scaling the data by 2 scales every distance from the mean by 2.

questions.prompt: Values 1, 2, 3 have frequencies 4, 5, 1. Find the mean.

questions.statement: The median is more affected by outliers than the mean.
questions.explanation: The mean uses every value’s size; the median depends only on position, so it is resistant to outliers.

questions.prompt: Match each measure to its definition.

pairs.right: sum of values ÷ number of values

questions.explanation: The first three measure centre; IQR measures spread.

questions.prompt: For grouped data, the class 10 ≤ x < 20 is represented in calculations by its mid-interval value:
questions.explanation: The mid-interval value is (10 + 20)/2 = 15, so the mean is an estimate.

questions.prompt: Put the steps for finding a median in order.
items: Count the number of values n
Read the value, averaging two if the position is between them
questions.explanation: Ordering first is essential.

questions.prompt: r = −0.92 describes:
questions.explanation: r close to −1 means points lie close to a line with negative gradient.

questions.statement: A strong correlation proves that one variable causes the other.
questions.explanation: Correlation does not imply causation; a third variable may affect both.

questions.text: The regression line of y on x is used to predict ___ from a given x.
questions.explanation: Use the y on x line only to predict y.

questions.prompt: The regression line is y = 2.4x + 15. Predict y when x = 10.
Exam score y and hours studied x fit y = 2.4x + 15. The gradient means:
options: each extra hour is associated with 2.4 more marks
a student who studies 0 hours scores 2.4
questions.explanation: The gradient is the change in y per unit increase in x.

questions.statement: Using a regression line from data with 0 ≤ x ≤ 12 to predict y at x = 50 is unreliable.
questions.explanation: This is extrapolation: the pattern may not continue outside the data.

questions.prompt: rₛ = 1 means:
options: the points lie on a straight line
the ranks of x and y agree exactly
questions.explanation: A perfect monotonic increasing relationship gives rₛ = 1 even if it is curved.

questions.prompt: Match each value of r to its description.
questions.explanation: The sign gives direction; the size gives strength.

questions.prompt: Put the steps for Spearman’s rank correlation in order.
items: Rank the y-values, averaging tied ranks
Find the correlation coefficient of the ranks with the GDC
questions.explanation: rₛ is Pearson’s r calculated on ranks.

questions.prompt: When is Spearman’s rank preferred to Pearson’s r?
options: When the data lie exactly on a line
When x and y have the same units
When the relationship is monotonic but not linear
questions.explanation: Spearman measures monotonic relationships and is less affected by outliers.
